ckd-vs-skd-vs-fg-floodlight.title: CKD vs. SKD vs. FG: Choosing the right delivery format for LED floodlights in Southeast Asia
ckd-vs-skd-vs-fg-floodlight.standfirst: A buyer's guide to cutting landed cost, clearing customs faster, and keeping final quality in your own hands.
ckd-vs-skd-vs-fg-floodlight.meta: 6 min read | Format: FG · SKD · CKD
ckd-vs-skd-vs-fg-floodlight.description: FG, SKD and CKD delivery formats for LED floodlights in Southeast Asia: how each one affects duty, shipping volume, labor and time-to-market — with a worked 200W floodlight example.

blocks.content: What FG, SKD and CKD actually mean
If you're importing LED floodlights into Southeast Asia, three shipping terms decide how much you pay — and how much work you take on:

**FG (Fully Good / Finished Goods)** — the complete, ready-to-sell product.
**SKD (Semi-Knocked-Down)** — partly assembled modules shipped together.
**CKD (Completely-Knocked-Down)** — every part shipped disassembled for local assembly.

The choice is rarely "which one is best." It's about **where you want to pay your money: in the factory, or in your own warehouse.** Done right, CKD can cut your landed cost by 15–30% while giving you more control over the final product. Done wrong, it turns your warehouse into a confusing pile of screws and heat sinks.

This guide breaks the three formats down side by side, using a **200W LED floodlight** as a concrete example, and explains why more Southeast Asian importers are moving toward CKD.
The three formats at a glance

FG (Finished Goods)	SKD (Semi-Knocked-Down)	CKD (Completely-Knocked-Down)
What you receive	Fully assembled, tested, boxed	Pre-assembled modules (e.g., LED board + driver mounted)	Every component loose: housing, LED module, driver, lens, screws
Who assembles	Factory (China)	You (light final assembly)	You (full assembly)
Assembly level	100% done	~50–70% done	0% done
Labor cost	Paid in China	Split	Mostly your local labor
Import duty	Highest (full product value)	Medium	Often lowest (parts classified separately)
Shipping volume	Bulkiest (empty space in boxes)	Medium	Most compact (flat-packed)
Quality control	Factory-controlled	Shared	In your hands
Time to shelf	Fastest (plug & sell)	Medium	Slowest (setup required)
Best for	Small orders, quick launches, no local setup	Testing the market, phased approach	Established buyers, high volume, cost leadership
A concrete example — the 200W LED floodlight
Let's break a 200W LED floodlight down into what actually arrives in each format. This makes the difference tangible.
FG — the "plug-and-sell" option
You receive a sealed box with the complete floodlight inside — housing closed, LED board mounted, driver wired, lens sealed, tested, and ready to power on.

**Pros:** Zero setup. Your team unpacks and sells.
**Cons:** You pay for Chinese labor, you pay duty on the full finished product, and a bulky finished lamp wastes shipping space (the empty cavity inside every fixture still costs you freight).
../assets/img/led_bulbs.png
SKD — the "half-way" option

The manufacturer ships **pre-built modules**: the LED light engine (LED board already mounted on its heat sink), the driver already wired to a connector, and the housing. Your team does the final snap-together: mount the module into the housing, close the lens, seal it, run a quick test.

**Pros:** Balance of lower duty and lower labor, with less assembly skill required.
**Cons:** Still pays duty on semi-finished assemblies, and you inherit some final-assembly quality risk.
CKD — the "full control" option
You receive **flat-packed kits**: separate cartons of die-cast housings, LED modules, drivers, lenses, screws, gaskets, and brackets. Your line assembles the entire fixture from scratch.

**Pros:** Lowest duty (components are classified as parts, often at lower tariff rates), most compact shipping (flat-packed = 3–4× more units per container), and full quality control in your hands.
**Cons:** You need a trained assembly line, tooling, and a QC process.

../assets/img/skd-kit-flood.png
flood 型号

Real-world math
A 200W floodlight in FG might fill a 20-ft container with ~2,500 units. The same fixture in CKD flat-packing can push 7,000–9,000 units per container, because you eliminate the empty cavity and stacked void. That volume difference alone can drop your per-unit freight by more than half.
Why Southeast Asia is moving toward CKD
Southeast Asia has the exact conditions that make CKD attractive:

**Lower local labor cost.** Assembly wages in Vietnam, Indonesia, the Philippines, or Thailand are a fraction of Chinese factory labor. You capture that gap when you assemble locally.
**Import duty relief.** Many ASEAN countries (and preferential trade arrangements) impose lower tariffs on components than on finished lamps. CKD lets you split the classification.
**"Made locally" positioning.** For government tenders, projects, and B2B buyers, a locally assembled product often carries compliance or localization advantages.
**Cash-flow flexibility.** You buy parts and assemble to order, rather than holding capital in finished goods inventory that may not match demand.
The trade-off is real: CKD demands **discipline.** You need a bill of materials (BOM), an assembly SOP, and a QC checklist — or you'll turn savings into returns.
Making the choice — a simple decision path
Ask yourself four questions:

**What's my monthly volume?** Under ~500 units — stay with FG. 500–3,000 — consider SKD. Over 3,000 — CKD usually wins.
**Do I have (or can I build) a competent assembly team?** If no, CKD's savings will leak into rework and defects.
**Can I absorb slower time-to-market?** CKD adds 2–4 weeks for setup and first-batch learning.
**How does my country classify components vs. finished lamps?** Confirm the actual tariff difference before committing — this is where the real money is.
If you answered "high volume + yes to assembly + yes to patience + confirmed tariff gap," CKD is almost certainly your best path.
Common pitfalls to avoid with CKD

**No BOM discipline.** Missing one screw or gasket stops the whole line. Your supplier should provide a precise, versioned BOM and a photo-based packing list.
**Skipping incoming QC.** Inspect a sample of every component lot on arrival — a defective driver caught early costs you minutes, not a returned shipment.
**Underestimating tooling.** You'll need torque drivers, a testing rig (or a simple power-on + lumen check), and sealant. Budget for it upfront.
**Ignoring after-sales parts.** Keep a safety stock of drivers and lenses, because you're now your own warranty service center.
The bottom line
There's no single "best" delivery format — there's the format that matches **your volume, your capability, and your tariff environment.**

**FG** is for speed and simplicity.
**SKD** is a pragmatic middle step.
**CKD** is how serious, high-volume buyers in Southeast Asia turn a commodity import into a margin and a local advantage.

The buyers winning in this market aren't the ones who pick a format and never change. They're the ones who **graduate** — start with FG to enter fast, move to SKD to test local assembly, and scale into CKD once volume justifies the investment.

faq.q: How does the driver behave on a 440 V feeder?
faq.a: The YE-01 driver holds constant current from roughly 165 to 280 Vac. Below that it folds back to protect itself; above 290 Vac output is deliberately derated, so a fixture running on a 440 V feeder will light up and stay stable — it simply will not deliver full rated wattage. On our 100 W high bay test unit, output settled near 38 W at 440 Vac . We publish the full 22-point grid rather than a single headline voltage because that is the honest picture: wide input means the light survives, not that it performs identically everywhere. The street-light wattage curves are measured once a project spec is fixed.

faq.q: Can one driver cover both the 40 W and the 60 W version?
faq.a: Yes. Both wattages sit on the same single-board driver; the difference is the output current setting and the LED board string configuration. That means one driver reel and one assembly procedure covers your whole street-light range, which is usually the difference between holding two spare-part lines and holding one.

faq.q: What pole height and spacing does the 60 W version suit?
faq.a: Typically 6–8 m mounting height for secondary and residential roads. Type II distribution for carriageways up to about 9 m wide, Type III where the pole sits on one side and the beam has to reach further across. We do not publish a lux grid for a reference design, because spacing depends on your road class and local lighting code. Send us the road width, pole height and target lux level, and we will run the layout with you.

faq.q: IP65 or IP66 — which one do I actually need?
faq.a: IP65 protects against water jets; IP66 against powerful jets, such as driving rain at an exposed coastal or elevated site. For inland towns IP65 is normally enough and costs less. For coastal roads, or anywhere the housing faces monsoon wind directly, specify IP66 — the gasket and cable-gland cost difference is small next to a field failure.

faq.q: Does the housing survive salt spray and monsoon humidity?
faq.a: The body is die-cast aluminium with a powder coating, which is the right starting point for coastal installations. Salt-spray endurance depends on coating thickness and pretreatment, so we confirm the exact hours against your site conditions rather than quoting a generic number. If your project is within a few kilometres of the coast, tell us at inquiry stage and we will specify the coating accordingly.

faq.q: With 4 kV surge immunity, do I still need a separate SPD?
faq.a: For most urban distribution circuits, no — 4 kV on the driver covers the switching transients you normally see. For poles at the end of an overhead line, in high-lightning regions, or on the same circuit as large welding or pumping loads, we recommend an external surge protector at the pole. It is a low-cost part and it protects the whole fixture.

faq.q: Who files the certification in my country — you or me?
faq.a: You do, because registration schemes such as BIS, SIRIM, TISI and SNI require a locally registered entity as the applicant. Our job is to make that filing fast: we hand over the test data, BOM, driver specifications and technical file your lab and agent need. Filing as the registrant also means the certificate sits in your company name, which is worth more to you than a supplier’s certificate ever would be.

faq.q: Can the LED module or driver be replaced in the field?
faq.a: Yes — and this is the practical advantage of SKD construction. The LED board and the driver are separate assemblies held by screws and connectors, so a failed driver is a 10-minute swap by a technician with a screwdriver, not a fixture replacement. Both parts can be ordered separately in your maintenance quantities.

faq.q: What happens above 290 Vac on a 440 V supply?
faq.a: Constant current holds to roughly 290 Vac, then output folds back to protect the board. On our 100 W unit output settled near 38 W at 440 Vac : the fixture keeps running safely, it just will not deliver rated wattage. That behaviour is normal for any single-stage flyback and it is why we publish the measured 22-point grid. A supplier quoting only “100–440 Vac” without the derating curve is telling you half the story.

faq.q: Which mounting height does the 100 W unit suit?
faq.a: Typically 8–12 m in warehousing and logistics halls, 6–8 m in lower workshops and service bays. Narrower beam angles for high ceilings, wider for low ones. Mounting height and beam angle have to be chosen together — picking one without the other is the most common reason a high bay ends up with dark aisles. Send us the height and the target lux at floor level and we will match the optic.

faq.q: How hot does it run after 90 minutes?
faq.a: At 32 °C ambient and 230 Vac, both driver ICs settle at 82.5 °C while the EE16 transformer winding reaches 100.6 °C. At 265 Vac the winding climbs to 104.3 °C and becomes the real thermal limit — not the IC, as most buyers assume. Extrapolated to a 45 °C ambient that is about 117.3 °C, roughly 13 K below the Class B 130 °C ceiling. That headroom is the number to check before specifying this fixture in an unventilated roof space.

faq.q: Does 100 W replace a 250 W HPS one for one?
faq.a: Not by wattage alone. On delivered lumens a 100 W LED usually gets close to a 250 W high-pressure sodium lamp, but the number that decides whether your aisles stay lit is maintained lux at the working plane. That depends on mounting height, beam angle, luminaire efficiency and the maintenance factor your client accepts. Give us height and target lux; we will run the comparison rather than hand you a rule of thumb.

faq.q: What LED configuration is inside?
faq.a: 24 series × 6 parallel on 6 V SMD2835, 144 devices in total, driven at 144 V / 610 mA ±5 %. The series ratio is chosen so output voltage stays around 144 V while current stays moderate — that balance is what allows a single-board driver measuring 191.5 × 165 mm to carry the whole 100 W.

faq.q: What should I specify if the plant is hot or dusty?
faq.a: Actual ceiling temperature, first of all. Our thermal data was taken at 32 °C ambient; at 45 °C the winding sits near 117.3 °C, so a plant running hotter than that needs a different design, not a different sales claim. For dust, the two failure points are the housing gasket and the driver cavity. Tell us the environment and we will confirm the sealing level and the cleaning interval the fixture expects.

faq.q: Who files the certification in my country — you or me?
faq.a: You do. Registration schemes such as BIS, SIRIM, TISI and SNI require a locally registered entity as the applicant. We supply the test data, BOM, driver specifications and technical file that your lab and agent need to file quickly. The certificate then sits in your company name — an asset on your balance sheet, not a document you borrow from a supplier.

faq.q: Can the driver board be replaced on its own?
faq.a: Yes. The driver is a single board measuring 191.5 × 165 mm, mounted on standoffs and connected by plug-in leads, so it lifts out without disturbing the LED board or the optic. Keep a small stock of boards and a failed unit is a bench repair rather than a scrapped fixture.

faq.q: What happens above 290 Vac on a 440 V supply?
faq.a: Same platform behaviour as the high bay: constant current to about 290 Vac, then foldback. The fixture runs safely on a 440 V feeder but will not deliver its rated 50 W. On the 100 W version of this platform, measured output at 440 Vac settled near 38 W. We will run the equivalent curve for 50 W once a project wattage is fixed, so the number you quote is measured rather than extrapolated.

faq.q: Symmetric or asymmetric beam — which do I need for a facade?
faq.a: Asymmetric, in almost every facade and wall-wash case. A symmetric beam throws as much light into the sky and the neighbouring property as onto the surface you are lighting, which is both wasteful and the first thing a lighting consultant will object to. Symmetric optics still make sense for open yards and general area lighting where there is no surface to graze.

faq.q: How far does the 50 W version throw?
faq.a: Useful throw depends more on beam angle than on wattage. With a narrow optic, 50 W will put usable light on a surface 20–30 m away; with a wide optic the same fixture is better used within 8–12 m. Because we do not publish lux grids for a reference design, tell us the distance, the mounting height and the target illuminance and we will specify the optic instead of guessing.

faq.q: How do I control glare on a yard or sports pole?
faq.a: Three things, in order of effect: mount higher, use a narrower beam aimed below the horizontal, and add a shield or visor to the housing. Wattage is the last lever, not the first. If the pole also lights a road or neighbouring property, local light-trespass rules usually cap the upward component, so the optic and the aiming angle have to be chosen together.

faq.q: How hot does the 50 W version run?
faq.a: Our 50 W flood light thermal soak at 33 °C ambient put the EE16 transformer winding at 93.4 °C at 265 Vac , with the driver ICs lower still. That is roughly 11 K cooler than the 100 W high bay on the same platform, which is what you would expect from half the throughput. In a hot climate, add your site ambient to that rise before deciding whether the headroom is enough.

faq.q: What sealing level do I need for permanent outdoor mounting?
faq.a: IP65 as a baseline for wall and pole mounting under an eave; IP66 where the fixture takes wind-driven rain directly, which is most coastal and exposed sites. The cable entry, not the lens, is where water gets in when a fitting fails. Tell us the mounting orientation — horizontal, tilted or vertical — because it changes how water sits on the gasket.

faq.q: Who files the certification in my country — you or me?
faq.a: You do, as the locally registered applicant for schemes such as BIS, SIRIM, TISI or SNI. We provide the test data, BOM and technical file your lab needs, and we answer their technical questions directly so the filing does not stall on us.

faq.q: Can the LED board be swapped without replacing the fixture?
faq.a: Yes. The LED board and the 132 × 134.5 mm driver board are separate assemblies, each held by screws and plug-in connectors. A failed driver is a board swap in minutes; the housing, gasket and optic stay in service.

faq.q: Why 90–440 Vac when my grid is 220–240 V?
faq.a: Because the grid you are quoted is not the grid you get. Feeder voltage sags at the end of a line, rises at night when load drops, and swings hard when a large load switches nearby. A lamp rated only for 220–240 V works in the lab and fails in the field. The wide range also means one SKU covers every market in the region, which simplifies your own stock keeping.

faq.q: How does one driver BOM cover the whole 9–50 W range?
faq.a: Over-temperature protection is set by an external resistor rather than being fixed inside the IC. Change that resistor and the same board serves a different wattage, so you buy one driver in volume and configure it per SKU at assembly instead of carrying five part numbers.

faq.q: Why does THD below 15 % matter in practice?
faq.a: Because you are not the only load on the transformer. High harmonic distortion from lighting heats shared distribution transformers and neutral conductors, and utilities in several markets now check it at the connection point. Under 15 % at 230 Vac full load keeps a large lighting installation from becoming the reason a building fails a power quality inspection.

faq.q: Are the lamp bases included?
faq.a: Bases are an option, not standard: specify E27 or B22 and they ship with the kit. Most customers assembling locally prefer to source bases in-country, because they are bulky, cheap and easier to buy regionally than to ship from us.

faq.q: What does 105 lm/W mean for my market?
faq.a: It is a measured system figure for the series, not a chip datasheet number, so it is the value you can put in front of a utility or a tender specification. Whether it clears a particular energy-efficiency tier depends on the scheme — send us the tier you are targeting and we will confirm which wattages qualify.

faq.q: Who files the certification in my country — you or me?
faq.a: You do. BIS, SIRIM, TISI and SNI all require a locally registered applicant. We provide the test data, technical file and driver documentation your lab needs, and the resulting certificate stays in your name rather than ours.

faq.q: 2 ft or 4 ft — which should I stock?
faq.a: Stock both, but lead with 4 ft. It is the replacement size for the fluorescent battens already installed across the region, so it moves on compatibility rather than on being sold. 2 ft is the fitting for corridors, stairwells and small rooms where a 4 ft tube simply does not fit. It is a smaller volume but a very stable one.

faq.q: Why is the 20 W version less efficient than the 36 W?
faq.a: Driver overhead is roughly fixed while output scales with wattage, so the same board carries a larger share of its own consumption on the smaller lamp: ≥ 89 % at 20 W against ≥ 91 % at 36 W. It is worth knowing when you quote on running cost, because the 20 W unit is not simply two-thirds of the 36 W in efficiency terms.

faq.q: What does “no VCC cap, no COMP cap, no FB resistor” actually mean for me?
faq.a: It means three fewer components per driver, and those three are among the ones that drift with heat and age. Fewer parts means a shorter assembly step, a lower BOM, and fewer field returns that trace back to a capacitor drying out.

faq.q: Will it hold up on an unstable single-phase supply?
faq.a: That is what the 90–440 Vac range is for: sag at the end of a feeder, night-time overvoltage, and the dip when a large load starts nearby. Input is protected to 4 kV line-to-line, in line with the rest of the platform. If your grid regularly goes below 90 V or above 440 V, that is a different problem and worth telling us about.

faq.q: Who files the certification in my country — you or me?
faq.a: You do, as the locally registered applicant for BIS, SIRIM, TISI or SNI. We hand over the test data, BOM and technical file your lab needs, and answer their questions during review.

faq.q: Can the LED board be replaced without scrapping the housing?
faq.a: Yes. The tube and the driver are separate assemblies inside the housing, so a failure is a board or tube swap rather than a whole-fitting replacement. That matters for commercial buildings where the fittings are already installed and access is the expensive part.

faq.q: How long does it stay lit after a power cut?
faq.a: Run time is set by the battery pack against a maximum emergency drive current of 1 A, so it depends on which pack you specify rather than on the lamp alone. Tell us the run time your code requires and we will size the pack to match it. We do not quote a headline number for this, because a run time without a stated load and battery capacity is not a specification — it is a guess dressed up as one.

faq.q: How quickly does the pack recharge?
faq.a: The charging circuit is designed for short daily grid windows, so a brief period of mains power is enough to keep the pack ready. That suits markets where the supply is intermittent rather than off for a full day. Recharge time depends on pack capacity and on how deeply it was discharged, so confirm it against your duty cycle before quoting a figure to a customer.

faq.q: Is the battery pack included in the kit?
faq.a: Yes, when specified — “battery pack included in kit” is an option on this model. Many buyers choose to ship the lamp and the pack separately, which is cheaper on air freight and avoids dangerous-goods handling on the lamp itself.

faq.q: What protects the pack from being ruined?
faq.a: Overcharge protection cuts in at about 4.2 V and over-discharge at about 2.4 V. Both matter more than capacity in this product category: most emergency lamps fail early because the pack was left discharged, not because it was too small. Over-discharge protection is the one to ask about when you compare suppliers — it is often left out to save a few cents.

faq.q: Can it charge properly on a weak grid?
faq.a: The input stage charges correctly from 90 to 440 Vac, which covers sagging feeders and night-time overvoltage without damaging the charging circuit. Surge immunity is 4 kV line-to-line, consistent with the rest of the platform. Efficiency is above 87 % at 230 Vac input, so very little of the charging energy is lost as heat in a closed fitting.

faq.q: How do I ship a lamp with a lithium pack?
faq.a: Battery packs are regulated for air transport, so most customers ship lamps and packs separately and consolidate at destination. Tell us the destination and the mode and we will confirm which documents we can provide for that route. Do not assume a supplier’s generic certificate covers your lane — dangerous-goods rules differ by carrier and by route.
